ann_31.text: This part acts on 80 of 242 training patients (33%), only 9 of whom had heart disease; for the typical patient it acts on (a 45-year-old man with non-anginal chest pain, no ST depression and a maximum heart rate of 168 beats per minute), it slightly lowers the predicted risk, from about 4% to about 1% (on the training data only).

Through it, older age raises the predicted risk steadily up to about 56 years (between 45 and 61 years for different patients), then no further: for a typical patient, from about 12% at 42 years to about 28% at 66 years; this holds for most patients, but for patients with a reversible defect on the thallium scan it rises mostly in a jump (on the training data only).
This rise with age clearly happens only if the thallium scan shows no reversible defect (from about 12% to about 28%, while it stays at about 42% with a reversible defect).

Its rise with age is clearly larger if the maximum heart rate is above 152 beats per minute (from about 8% to about 27%, against about 18% to about 30% at or below 152); there it rises steadily up to about 58 years, then no further, for most patients, but for patients with a reversible defect on the thallium scan it rises mostly in a jump.
A higher maximum heart rate lowers it through this part in an uneven way across patients, from about 28% at 118 to about 22% at 175 beats per minute (on the training data only).
A higher maximum heart rate clearly lowers the predicted risk more, in an uneven way, without a reversible thallium defect (from about 32% to about 20%, against about 46% to about 40% with one).

ann_32.text: This part acts on 117 of 242 training patients (48%), and 78 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 58-year-old man with a flat ST segment, 1.4 mm of ST depression, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on the resting ECG and a reversible thallium defect), it slightly raises the predicted risk, from about 87% to about 90% (on the training data only).

Through it, a flat ST segment, more ST depression and higher cholesterol each change the predicted risk only slightly, and in an uneven way across patients for ST depression and cholesterol (on the training data only).

Across the whole model, higher cholesterol clearly raises the predicted risk steadily, and even more so if the ST segment is not flat (from about 18% to about 49%, against about 67% to about 88% with a flat ST segment).
The rise from more ST depression, slow at first, then faster, differs only slightly between patients with a flat ST segment (from about 75% to about 91%) and others (from about 28% to about 47%).

ann_33.text: This part acts on 121 of 242 training patients (50%), and 77 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 58-year-old man with 1.6 mm of ST depression, a flat ST segment, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on the resting ECG and a reversible thallium defect), it slightly raises the predicted risk, from about 89% to about 91% (on the training data only).
Through it, more ST depression on exercise raises a typical patient's predicted risk slowly at first, then faster, from about 28% at 0 mm to about 47% at 2.8 mm (on the training data only).
ST depression adds risk here only once it rises above about 0.8 mm: going from 0 to 3.5 mm moves a typical patient from about 28% to about 56% (on the training data only).

ann_34.text: For a typical patient, the model clearly gives a lower predicted risk of heart disease with typical angina (about 3%), non-anginal chest pain (about 5%) or atypical angina (about 14%) than with no chest pain symptoms (about 28%).

Each extra vessel coloured adds about the same: going from 0 to 2 vessels raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 28% to about 94%, flattening out near the top because it cannot go much higher, and a flat rather than upsloping ST segment at peak exercise raises it to about 77% (on the training data only).

Higher cholesterol and higher resting blood pressure raise it steadily: from about 18% at 193 mg/dL to about 49% at 308 mg/dL, and from about 19% at 110 mm Hg to about 43% at 155 mm Hg (on the training data only).
More ST depression on exercise raises it slowly at first, then faster, from about 28% at 0 mm to about 47% at 2.8 mm (on the training data only).

Older age raises it steadily up to about 54 years, then no further, from about 12% at 42 to about 28% at 66 years; this holds for most patients, but for a group of men with a reversible defect on the thallium scan it rises mostly in a jump (on the training data only).
Chest pain brought on by exercise and a reversible thallium defect each raise it to about 42% (on the training data only).

Being a woman lowers it from about 28% to about 3%, fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL lowers it to about 14%, and a higher maximum heart rate lowers it in an uneven way across patients, from about 32% at 118 to about 20% at 175 beats per minute (on the training data only).

The model has little data on three categories: a downsloping ST segment (17 patients; about 51%), an ST-T wave abnormality on the resting ECG (2 patients; about 46%) and a fixed defect on the thallium scan (15 patients; about 11%), all on the training data only.

ann_31.original: Heart-rate-reserve gate 1718 = ReLU(-0.812 - 1.490*age + 1.024*thalach - 0.762*thal:7 - 0.720*R3195), with relay R3195 = ReLU(0.981 + 1.073*thal:7). Hypothesis: 3195 is an always-on affine relay of thal:7 (thal:7 is one-hot, z-scored to {-0.769, 1.300}, so 3195 in {0.155, 2.376} > 0), which makes the gate's net thal:7 coefficient -1.535 and bias -1.518. The gate fires for patients whose achieved max heart rate is high for their age (thalach up, age down) AND who do NOT have a reversible thallium defect; its readout into the output is -0.582, so it is a protective (risk-lowering) term. EVIDENCE (train, n=242): 3195 is active for 100% of patients, so the gate reduces exactly to 1718 = ReLU(-1.518 - 1.490*age + 1.024*thalach - 1.535*thal:7). Active 33% overall: 51% of patients without a reversible defect vs 3% with one. Disease rate 11% when active vs 60% when inactive. Mean |sensitivity|: age 0.49 > thalach 0.34 > thal:7 (two copies) 0.25 each. Removing its readout drops train AUC 0.943 -> 0.938, the largest single nonlinear effect (readout logit SD 0.64). Supported.
ann_31.proposed: A part that acts on a third of patients, few of whom had heart disease; through it, older age raises the predicted risk up to about 56 years (between 45 and 61 years for different patients), and only without a reversible thallium defect, while a higher maximum heart rate lowers it.

ann_32.original: Flat-ST-slope gate 1476 = ReLU(0.257 + 1.145*slope:2 + 0.770*oldpeak - 0.374*C3464), with C3464 = ReLU(1.300 + 1.011*chol). Hypothesis: a one-sided risk detector that opens for patients with a flat peak-exercise ST segment (slope:2), its height scaled by ST depression (oldpeak) and reduced by cholesterol via an almost-always-active affine chol relay (3464 is zero only when z-chol < -1.29). Readout into output +0.225 (raises risk). EVIDENCE (train, n=242): 3464 is active for 93% (off only when z-chol < -1.29), so 1476 is nearly ReLU(-0.229 + 1.145*slope:2 + 0.770*oldpeak - 0.378*chol). Active for 98% of the 110 flat-slope patients vs 7% of the others, so it acts as a flat-slope indicator whose height rises with oldpeak (corr 0.69) and falls with cholesterol. Disease rate 67% when active vs 23% when inactive. Mean |sensitivity|: slope:2 0.55 > oldpeak 0.37 > chol 0.17. Removing its readout drops train AUC 0.943 -> 0.942 (logit SD 0.18). Supported. The negative chol term partly offsets chol's direct +0.613 edge for flat-slope patients; no clinical reading is offered for that.
ann_32.proposed: A part that acts on about half the patients and changes their predicted risk only slightly; through it, a flat ST segment, ST depression and cholesterol each have small effects.

ann_33.original: Oldpeak hinge pair: 1946 = ReLU(0.167 + 0.767*oldpeak) and 3284 = ReLU(-0.582 + 1.003*1946). Hypothesis: a convex piecewise-linear function of ST depression alone, with kinks at z-oldpeak = -0.218 (1946 opens) and 0.539 (3284 opens). Both exits read out positively (0.377 and 0.411), so beyond the second kink the logit slope in oldpeak roughly doubles: mild ST depression adds a little risk, marked ST depression adds much more. EVIDENCE (train, n=242): 1946 active 50% (disease rate 64%), 3284 active 24% (disease rate 79%). Contribution to the logit 0.377*1946 + 0.411*3284 has slope 0 below z-oldpeak -0.218, 0.289 between the kinks and 0.605 above 0.539. Mean |sensitivity| to oldpeak: 0.38 for 1946, 0.18 for 3284. Removing either readout changes train AUC by <= 0.001. Supported: a small convex ST-depression dose-response.
ann_33.proposed: ST depression on exercise above about 0.8 mm raises the predicted risk through this part.

ann_34.original: Root: logit z = -0.210 + LINEAR CORE - 0.582*age_hr_reserve_gate + 0.225*st_slope_chol_gate + 0.377*oldpeak_hinges[1946] + 0.411*oldpeak_hinges[3284]; prediction = sigmoid(z) (the genome output node is shown as ReLU, but for binary classification the evaluator applies a sigmoid, so z is a logistic score). LINEAR CORE (16 direct input->output edges, z-scored inputs): ca +1.68, cp:4 +0.99, sex:0 -0.74, chol +0.61, slope:2 +0.49, slope:1 -0.47, trestbps +0.47, sex:1 +0.45, cp:2 +0.42, fbs:1 -0.31, thal:7 +0.29, exang:1 +0.28, thal:6 -0.28, cp:1 -0.18, thalach -0.10, restecg:1 +0.07. The signs mostly match cardiology: more fluoroscopy-coloured vessels (ca), asymptomatic chest pain (cp:4), male sex, higher cholesterol and resting BP, flat ST slope and exertional angina raise risk, and upsloping ST (slope:1) lowers it. Exceptions are cp:2 +0.42 and fbs:1 -0.31, which run against the usual clinical direction and are left unexplained. Eight inputs are unused (cp:3, fbs:0, restecg:0, restecg:2, exang:0, slope:3, thal:3, thal:4). Age and oldpeak have no direct edge: they act only through the gates. COMPOSITION: purely additive in the logit. The three children add three nonlinear corrections to the linear core: (1) age_hr_reserve_gate, a protective ReLU that is on when max heart rate is high for the patient's age and there is no reversible thallium defect; (2) st_slope_chol_gate, a flat-ST-slope detector scaled up by oldpeak and down by cholesterol; (3) oldpeak_hinges, a convex two-kink dose-response in ST depression. The children share no hidden nodes. They are coupled only through shared input features (thal:7, thalach, chol and slope:2 also have direct edges, and oldpeak feeds both (2) and (3)). EVIDENCE (train, n=242): full model AUC 0.943, acc 0.884 (sigmoid(z) reproduces the evaluator exactly). Linear core alone gives AUC 0.930, so the nonlinear children add +0.013. parts.name: age_hr_reserve_gate
parts.original_hypothesis: Heart-rate-reserve gate 1718 = ReLU(-0.812 - 1.490*age + 1.024*thalach - 0.762*thal:7 - 0.720*R3195), with relay R3195 = ReLU(0.981 + 1.073*thal:7). Hypothesis: 3195 is an always-on affine relay of thal:7 (thal:7 is one-hot, z-scored to {-0.769, 1.300}, so 3195 in {0.155, 2.376} > 0), which makes the gate's net thal:7 coefficient -1.535 and bias -1.518. The gate fires for patients whose achieved max heart rate is high for their age (thalach up, age down) AND who do NOT have a reversible thallium defect; its readout into the output is -0.582, so it is a protective (risk-lowering) term. EVIDENCE (train, n=242): 3195 is active for 100% of patients, so the gate reduces exactly to 1718 = ReLU(-1.518 - 1.490*age + 1.024*thalach - 1.535*thal:7). Active 33% overall: 51% of patients without a reversible defect vs 3% with one. Disease rate 11% when active vs 60% when inactive. Mean |sensitivity|: age 0.49 > thalach 0.34 > thal:7 (two copies) 0.25 each. Removing its readout drops train AUC 0.943 -> 0.938, the largest single nonlinear effect (readout logit SD 0.64). Supported.

parts.name: oldpeak_hinges
parts.original_hypothesis: Oldpeak hinge pair: 1946 = ReLU(0.167 + 0.767*oldpeak) and 3284 = ReLU(-0.582 + 1.003*1946). Hypothesis: a convex piecewise-linear function of ST depression alone, with kinks at z-oldpeak = -0.218 (1946 opens) and 0.539 (3284 opens). Both exits read out positively (0.377 and 0.411), so beyond the second kink the logit slope in oldpeak roughly doubles: mild ST depression adds a little risk, marked ST depression adds much more. EVIDENCE (train, n=242): 1946 active 50% (disease rate 64%), 3284 active 24% (disease rate 79%). Contribution to the logit 0.377*1946 + 0.411*3284 has slope 0 below z-oldpeak -0.218, 0.289 between the kinks and 0.605 above 0.539. Mean |sensitivity| to oldpeak: 0.38 for 1946, 0.18 for 3284. Removing either readout changes train AUC by <= 0.001. Supported: a small convex ST-depression dose-response.
variables: ST depression during exercise (compared with rest)

parts.name: st_slope_chol_gate
parts.original_hypothesis: Flat-ST-slope gate 1476 = ReLU(0.257 + 1.145*slope:2 + 0.770*oldpeak - 0.374*C3464), with C3464 = ReLU(1.300 + 1.011*chol). Hypothesis: a one-sided risk detector that opens for patients with a flat peak-exercise ST segment (slope:2), its height scaled by ST depression (oldpeak) and reduced by cholesterol via an almost-always-active affine chol relay (3464 is zero only when z-chol < -1.29). Readout into output +0.225 (raises risk). EVIDENCE (train, n=242): 3464 is active for 93% (off only when z-chol < -1.29), so 1476 is nearly ReLU(-0.229 + 1.145*slope:2 + 0.770*oldpeak - 0.378*chol). Active for 98% of the 110 flat-slope patients vs 7% of the others, so it acts as a flat-slope indicator whose height rises with oldpeak (corr 0.69) and falls with cholesterol. Disease rate 67% when active vs 23% when inactive. Mean |sensitivity|: slope:2 0.55 > oldpeak 0.37 > chol 0.17. Removing its readout drops train AUC 0.943 -> 0.942 (logit SD 0.18). Supported. The negative chol term partly offsets chol's direct +0.613 edge for flat-slope patients; no clinical reading is offered for that.

ann_31.text: This part acts on 80 of 242 training patients (33%).
For a typical patient it acts on, it slightly lowers the predicted risk of heart disease from about 4% without this part to about 1% with it (on the training data only).
In the training data, 9 of these 80 patients had heart disease.

A higher age clearly raises the predicted risk of heart disease, but only if thallium stress test result is something other than a reversible defect on the thallium scan (steadily up to about 54 years, then no further for patients with thallium stress test result other than a reversible defect on the thallium scan): for a typical patient, age going from 42 years to 66 years moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 12% to about 28% if thallium stress test result is something other than a reversible defect on the thallium scan, and from about 42% to about 42% if the thallium scan shows a reversible defect.

Other effects: a higher age raises it steadily up to about 56 years (between 45 years and 61 years for different patients), then no further for most patients, but for patients with a reversible defect on the thallium scan it moves mostly in a jump; age depending on maximum heart rate raises it steadily up to about 58 years, then no further for most patients, but for patients with a reversible defect on the thallium scan it moves mostly in a jump; a higher maximum heart rate lowers it in an uneven way; maximum heart rate depending on thallium stress test result lowers it in an uneven way (on the training data only).

Smaller effects, each changing the predicted value only slightly: maximum heart rate past about 165 beats per minute lowers it in an uneven way; a reversible defect on the thallium scan (rather than any other thallium stress test result) raises it; age past about 56 years raises it steadily up to about 56 years (between 45 years and 61 years for different patients), then no further (on the training data only). The model has little data on some of these: only 15 training patients (patients with a fixed defect on the thallium scan whose curve has a fold) and 3 training patients (of them, patients already past their fold).

ann_32.text: This part acts on 117 of 242 training patients (48%).
For a typical patient it acts on, it slightly raises the predicted risk of heart disease from about 87% without this part to about 90% with it (on the training data only).
In the training data, 78 of these 117 patients had heart disease.

A higher serum cholesterol clearly raises the predicted risk of heart disease, and even more so if slope of the ST segment at peak exercise is something other than a flat ST segment (steadily for patients with slope of the ST segment at peak exercise other than a flat ST segment): for a typical patient, serum cholesterol going from 193 mg/dL (5.0 mmol/L) to 308 mg/dL (8.0 mmol/L) moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 18% to about 49% if slope of the ST segment at peak exercise is something other than a flat ST segment, and from about 67% to about 88% if the ST segment is flat at peak exercise.
